reference.device: Turns a vendor release into a job description: names the role a small business has to fill, then attaches it to a named product shipping a fixed count of prebuilt workflows.
reference.why_reference: The only reel in the top 150 that says small business and still lands 35 saves per 1,000 against an author median of 17,919.

hook: Somebody in your company now owns AI. Nobody wrote the job.
problem: The person told to figure out AI for a team of five to fifty has no brief, no budget line and no definition of done. They open a chat window on Monday and guess.
solution: We write that job in public, one repeated workflow at a time: pick the workflow, fragment it, draw the AI boundary, name who approves. Human review step: Michael signs every verdict before it ships.
cta: Write the one sentence your AI owner is missing: which workflow, whose approval, what a wrong answer costs.
why_now: A vendor shipped prebuilt small-business workflows on 11 Aug 2026 and that reel is still the highest saving small-business reel in the window; the open question this fortnight is who operates them.
utility: A three-line role definition the viewer writes in the last beat.
proof: Our filled-in three-line role definition for the radar workflow, on screen, with Michael named as approver.

reference.device: Credential first, then a numbered checklist where every line names the cost of getting it wrong. The reason to forward is the consequence, not the tip.
reference.why_reference: Highest saves per 1,000 in the entire top 150 and second highest shares per 1,000; the strongest single device in the data.

hook: Before AI touches a process, we write down what a wrong answer costs.
problem: A team lead connects a chat model to something customer-facing and learns the cost of an error after the error.
solution: Our four-question filter run out loud on one process, with a cost line against each answer. Human review step: Max reads the filter, Michael signs the sheet.
cta: Take the workflow you ran three times last week and write one line: what does one wrong output cost, in money or in trust.
why_now: The 7 September radar run proposed nine cards and struck four against exactly these four questions.
utility: The four-question sheet as a file, with our own four cost lines filled in.
proof: Screenshot of the nine proposed cards with the four struck rows visible, from the cards table of radar-0907.db.

reference.device: The same-input comparison, shown rather than claimed. Same model, same prompt, without the wrapper, in one cut.
reference.why_reference: Beat its author's median by 2.24 times on a small base five days ago, with no giveaway and no trade for a reply.

hook: Same request, twice. One went through a chat box, one went through our workflow.
problem: A manager tries a model on a real task, gets a fluent paragraph, cannot tell whether it is right, and concludes AI is not ready.
solution: We run one real request from our own week twice on camera: bare chat, then the same request inside our workflow with the source attached. Human review step: Michael reads both outputs and marks the unsupported sentence.
tool: the chat model we already pay for, plus our own workflow file
cta: Take one request you sent to a chat window last week and run it again with the source document attached. Compare the two answers.
why_now: Three of the freshest reels in the window, 1 and 2 September, react to a new model version; this piece answers them with the opposite claim.
utility: The two outputs side by side as a screenshot, plus the one-line instruction that made the difference.
proof: Both runs recorded on our own screen, same prompt, same model, timestamped, with the unsupported sentence circled.

reference.device: Price arithmetic as the whole story, including the cost that does not go away: the incumbent price band, the bill that grows with success, and the honest hosting and setup cost of the free alternative.
reference.why_reference: 27.8 times its author's median and 54 saves per 1,000, earned by naming the ongoing cost instead of hiding it.

hook: Our weekly AI run cost two dollars and twelve cents. Here is the rest of the bill.
problem: A leader is quoted a subscription price and budgets that number, then meets the setup hours, run cost, review minutes and one wrong output.
solution: We open our spend log on screen: 623 data requests and 12.46 dollars to build the radar 1 to 3 September, then 2.12 dollars for the 7 September run over 106 accounts and 1,260 reels, 78 minutes wall clock. Human review step: Max owns the run, Michael reviews the output; review time is marked to measure.
tool: our own radar, built on a data API charged per request
cta: Open your last AI invoice and add the two lines it does not show: setup hours and review minutes.
why_now: The first fully automatic run happened on 7 September, so a weekly figure exists for the first time and can be shown as a receipt.
utility: Our spend log as a screenshot, and a five-line cost sheet the viewer copies.
proof: Screenshot of the spend table showing 623 units at 12.46 and 106 units at 2.12, plus a stopwatch on one review pass to fill the missing line.

reference.device: Ours: name the search, show what it returns, then show what was needed; the gap is measured, not asserted.
reference.why_reference: Derived from topics.csv and top-reels.csv: AI in a specific business process has 29 scored reels, median score 0.473 and zero of the top 100, while AI agency as a business has 80 reels and 5 of the top 100 and Design and websites via AI 117 reels and 9. Three reels from one agency account hold six of the top 15 rows.

hook: You looked for AI help with your process. What you found was somebody selling an agency.
problem: The operations lead of a small firm searches for how AI fits one repeated process and the feed answers with income offers and agency funnels; next quarter the process still eats the same hours.
solution: One repeated workflow on the table, fragmented into inputs, outputs, decisions and risks, with the point where the model stops marked. Human review step: Michael owns the fragmentation sheet and Max builds only what survives it.
cta: Take the workflow you ran three times last week and fill four columns: input, output, decision, risk.
why_now: The 7 September snapshot is the first scored across 106 accounts and confirms that zero of the top 100 reels sit in our own topic.
utility: The fragmentation sheet as a page, with our radar workflow filled in as the worked example.
verdict: Teardown verdict card: KEEP collection and drafting as AI-assisted, KILL the automatic send, acceptance stays human-owned
proof: Our own fragmentation sheet for the radar, photographed, with the AI boundary drawn on the page by hand.

reference.device: Name the easy part, then name precisely what the model cannot do: it knows how to cut, it does not know which moment matters, because it has no context.
reference.why_reference: 32.6 shares and 56.0 saves per 1,000, the best combined pair in the top 150 outside the checklist reel, on a mid-sized account with no giveaway. Already chosen as reference by our own radar, card 1 of week 2026-09-03.

hook: Our tool ranked nine ideas this Monday. A person cut four of them.
problem: A team automates a selection step, trusts the ranking, and publishes something the company should not have said. Ranking is not deciding.
solution: We show the run: 1,260 reels collected, 1,255 scored, 1,156 through the entry gate, 97 taken apart frame by frame, nine cards proposed. Human review step: Michael decides, and the reason is written next to each removal.
tool: our own radar, scoring each reel against its own author's median rather than against the crowd
cta: Find the step where a tool proposes and nobody records why the proposal was rejected. Start recording it.
why_now: The 7 September run is the first that proposed and struck cards with no person in the loop until the review point.
utility: The nine proposals and four removals as a screenshot, plus the rule list that did the removing.
proof: The cards export for week 2026-09-07 showing nine rows and four struck, plus a screen recording of one removal being written.

reference.device: The bounded test window: tested for the last 24 hours, one exact prompt on screen, the version named, plus one setup detail the viewer would miss.
reference.why_reference: Four times its author's median within a day of a version landing, on saves. Also the clearest example of what we do not copy: a revenue claim with no baseline, closed by trading a reply for a file.

reference.device: Same week, same trigger: a version release turned into a workaround story.
reference.why_reference: Supporting evidence that the version release is the fortnight's repeated question.

hook: A new model version landed last week. Here is the one step it changed in our week.
problem: Every release resets the team's confidence; the lead asks whether to switch and nobody ran the old and the new on the same task.
solution: We run one fixed task from our own week, unchanged, on both versions, and report the one step where the output differed and the one where it did not. Human review step: Michael reads both and writes the verdict condition.
tool: named at shoot time: the exact model versions we ran, both of them
cta: Keep one fixed task and one fixed input. Run it on every version you are asked to switch to, before you switch.
why_now: Three reels in the freshest part of the window, 1 and 2 September, react to the same version. The Radar rule asks whether a topic survives three to seven days; this one does and then decays.
utility: Our fixed-task file, so the viewer has a test to reuse on the next release.
proof: Both runs on our own screen with the version string visible and a stopwatch on each.

reference.device: End-to-end outcome narration with the frictions listed as removals: find local businesses without a website, build a demo, send a personalized email, book the meeting. No proof at any step.
reference.why_reference: Second highest multiple of an author's median in the whole set, and the account that makes our own topic read as a sales funnel.

hook: This pitch automates finding a lead, writing a demo and sending it. One of those steps we do not automate.
problem: A small services firm wires up outbound and finds the failure mode late: a wrong output leaves under the company name, to a stranger, and cannot be recalled.
solution: The map on screen, CURRENT, AI LAYER, VERDICT. Research and drafting go to the model. Human review step: Michael presses send, because the cost of error is a customer who never replies again.
tool: named at shoot time for the research step only; the send step uses no tool
cta: In your outbound process, mark the last step before something leaves the building and write the name of the person who owns it.
why_now: The reel returns in both snapshots and the pattern repeats across the niche's top rows this fortnight. The demand is proven and the honest version is missing.
utility: The three-column map as a file, and the one-line rule for where a send stops.
verdict: Teardown verdict card: KEEP the research fragment, TEST the drafting fragment, KILL the automatic send
proof: Our own run of the research fragment on ten real companies with a count of the rows that came back wrong. If nothing comes back wrong, the piece does not ship.

reference.device: The time budget: intent converted into a scheduled slot, and the artifact made saveable. We take the time budget and refuse the list.
reference.why_reference: Highest multiple of an author's median in the whole set and 66.7 saves per 1,000, without a trade for a reply.

reference.device: The giveaway device in its cleanest form: a free, finite, self-paced artifact described in full before any call to action.
reference.why_reference: Supporting: shows the saveable artifact working at 42.9 saves per 1,000 even at the author's own median volume.

hook: Every line we publish is read by a machine before a person sees it.
problem: Any team with a style rule, a compliance line or a banned claim relies on a person remembering it at the end of a long day. The rule is written once and enforced never.
solution: We run our own pre-publication check on this very script: banned list, hook length, punctuation rule, failures returned. Human review step: Michael checks the one thing it cannot, whether the claim is true.
tool: our own copy checker, a small script over a written rule list
cta: Write down the three things you always fix by hand in outgoing copy. That list is the check.
why_now: The rule list was finalized on 8 September and the script now runs on every piece we ship, including this plan.
utility: The rule list as a file the viewer copies, and the run output on screen with its error count.
proof: A recorded run of the check on this content plan showing the error count before and after, and one error it misses on purpose.

reference.device: A numbered line with a named cost on each.
Price arithmetic that includes the cost that does not go away.
Proof shown in one cut rather than asserted.
Name the judgment the model does not have.

shared_trait: Every one hands the viewer a number or a comparison they can check themselves, and none requires trusting the author.
hook: Five lines tell you what one AI workflow costs you in a week.
problem: A leader approves a workflow on the subscription price alone, then meets the setup hours, the per-run charge, the review minutes and the price of one wrong output.
solution: The five-line cost sheet filled in live on our own radar: build cost 12.46 dollars over 623 data requests, weekly run 2.12 dollars over 106 accounts, wall clock 78 minutes, review minutes to measure, cost of one wrong card to measure. Human review step: Michael reads the sheet before any workflow gets a second week.
tool: the cost sheet itself, one page
cta: Fill the five lines for the workflow you ran three times last week. Stop at the line you cannot fill; that line is your next measurement.
why_now: The 7 September run is the first with a real weekly figure attached, and the niche is arguing about model prices without counting the other four lines.
utility: The five-line sheet as a file, with our numbers in it and two lines honestly empty.
proof: A stopwatch on one full review pass to fill the review line, and one deliberately wrong card costed in minutes of rework.
